title: Recording introduction and setup
description: Dale Anderson identifies the interview as being with Eva Jannusch in Kellogg, Idaho, on July 30, 1975. Most of this opening consists of repeated recording announcements and setup chatter rather than sustained subject matter.

title: Husband working away; wartime separation
description: Eva explains that she moved to Spokane while her husband worked down in Princeton because the woods paid much better than Spokane jobs. She says she disliked the separation, and Dale asks what she did with the time she otherwise would have spent with him.

title: Keeping busy in Spokane; friendship; Joy's schooling
description: Eva says she cleaned house, worked in a hospital, and became close to a neighbor who remembered her through Harold Luke, with whom she visited and went downtown. She also recalls that Joy started school at Avon in Spokane and stayed there until the family moved to Kellogg when Joy was in sixth grade.

title: Changes in education; school consolidation
description: Eva contrasts schooling in her youth with modern education, noting single teachers, book work, and pencil-and-paper lessons versus subject teachers, labs, experiments, and cooking. She thinks education is more liberal now, and on consolidation she chiefly remembers the prospect of her daughter riding a bus from Fernwood to St. Mary's.

title: Uses of the interview; taxes; government projects
description: Dale explains that the interview will go to the University of Idaho archives for research use. Eva then discusses her husband's dislike of government projects and high taxes, his sense that too few support too many, and her own more mixed view that people still have to be taken care of.

title: Old-time neighborly aid; welfare and work
description: Eva recalls a time when neighbors helped a local family in need but also pressured men who were able to work to do so. She suggests that kind of local enforcement is no longer possible, even though she does not simply reject helping people.

title: Modern conveniences; parenting and children's behavior
description: Asked about modern life, Eva says she has no complaint about modern conveniences but believes parents should watch children more closely and respond when problems arise. Drawing on her experience renting houses and having children in her yard, she argues that parents should talk with children, keep them out of bad environments, and expect them to report serious problems.

title: Present life compared with the past
description: Eva says she more or less goes along with life as it is now rather than preferring the past outright. She recalls that her own parents were strict and that her daughter also regarded her as strict about watching her friendships and knowing where she was.
